extracted.intended_audience: theatre critics, actors, dramatists, and literate theatre-going public
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging theatrical performance and dramatic writing, drawn from a critical essay on Edwin Forrest's acting. Emphasizes fidelity of detail, truthfulness of characterization, vocal and physical technique, and evaluation within genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and unity of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing seemed wanting, nothing seemed superfluous. Every tone, every glance, every gesture, every step, contributed towards shaping out the ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance should exhibit microscopic fidelity like a pre-Raphaelite picture: each element must serve the whole, avoiding excess or omission. Example: stage picture formed by cumulative small details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness to the audience / subtlety of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: To appreciate it as it deserved there was required an audience of psychologists, critically interested in the study of human nature; the general multitude must feel it rather dull and tiresome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some performances are deliberately subtle and demand a discerning audience; critics should judge expected subtlety rather than condemn for being 'dull' to general tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiated portrayal of age and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Forrest made distinctions in his rendering of old age as seen respectively in Richelieu, in Lear, and in Febro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old age (or any character trait) should be rendered differently according to each character's psychology: e.g., Lear's broken gigantic power; Richelieu's half-simulated decadence; Febro's hale, honorable age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions as indications of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: His very actions are unmistakable indications of his thoughts; the last scene of the tragedy deserves to stand alone as a picture of suffering age in which past energy and passion spasmodically assert themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External behaviour onstage must reliably reflect internal psychology — gestures and movement should be intelligible signs of thought and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity versus simulation
rubrics_metrics.description: One feels from the very manner of the artist that this is but partially real,—that a moment of success may kindle into new life the man prostrated by bodily weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should distinguish genuine, internally-motivated portrayal from half-simulated effects; true art suggests latent life rather than mere mannered pose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revelation of inner emotional life / humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: He uplifts the veil, tears away the mask, and exhibits the tenderness which...is intermixed with the iron in the mine where his intellect sinks the shaft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A powerful performance reveals the actor's humanity and inner life (not mere technique), giving audiences access to the character's heart and moral complexity, as in 'Broker of Bogota.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility and appropriateness of vocal and stylistic delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: The ponderous gave way to the romantic, declamation to conversational ease, monotone to graceful variety...reading over the letter...first time rapid, half-conscious; second time slow, careful, soliloquizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An actor should adapt vocal style and manner (from declamation to conversational ease, from monotone to variety), using nuanced shifts (e.g., repeated lines read differently) to convey changing states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical and costumed transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The transformation he underwent, as shown by his picture when costumed for the character, is a surprising evidence of his true dramatic faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costume and physical presentation should convincingly transform the actor into the role, supporting character believability rather than distracting from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to uplift, teach, and moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Many passages exemplify the high mission of the drama to refresh, to teach, and to uplift those who submit themselves to its influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama may have an educative or uplifting end; an interpreter who breathes 'glorious sentiments' and communicates moral or emotional truths is fulfilling a central dramatic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to evoke strong audience emotion and sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jack Cade of Forrest stirred the great passions in the bosom of the people, swept the chords of their elementary sympathies with tempestuous and irresistible power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A performance should be capable of moving audiences deeply — eliciting tears, sympathy, or righteous anger — by connecting with elemental sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layering and simultaneity of complex emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: He utters this speech in a manner which appears to melt wonder, musing, scorn, and threatening into one simultaneous expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skilled actors compress multiple affective attitudes into a single delivery to create psychologically rich moments; tonal and facial subtleties should convey overlapping emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contrast to heighten character
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic scenes occur, where the stern revolutionist, burning to avenge the hoarded injuries of his class, unbends in tender endearments. These two phases of his character heightened each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasting moods (tender domesticity vs. revolutionary fury) should be presented to produce a fuller, more persuasive character; contrasts amplify dramatic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical presence as moral and dramatic statement
rubrics_metrics.description: He seemed an avatar of avenging Providence as, hurling the base lord back, he loomed above him, with uplifted dagger, his grand physical and moral superiority saying, as plainly as speech, 'Heaven, not heraldry, makes noble men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical stature, movement, and presence onstage should communicate moral meanings and social relations — the body can speak as loudly as words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate performance by truth and power in its own kind
rubrics_metrics.description: It is to be rightly judged from its truth and power in its own kind and range; for that is all that the player professes to exhibit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should assess an actor or play according to standards appropriate to its genre and aims, not by unfair comparisons to different kinds of art or moral preconceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of morally ambiguous or violent characters when truthful
rubrics_metrics.description: The implacable animosity of Cade...are not beautiful, but may be edifying...such a character is far more noble and wholesome than any of those common types...made up of timid imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals of brutal or vengeful figures can be morally and aesthetically valid if they are truthful and powerful; critics should not reject such depictions solely on ethical distaste if they illuminate justice or human nature.
